I think that when we start to see ourselves as perfect or even that we can't change will actually cause more problems that one will have to deal with later. Change is extremely hard, but little adjustments can make a difference in the slightest things. For instance, I have little to no filter when I get angry so I'm really trying to restrain what I say and think before I actually verbalize what I mean. But I usually go right back to the way I've always been and go apeshit. We all are a work in progress, it's just a matter of progress we want to work on.

Yeah, I have a tendency to point out the areas I disagree with or make a qualification on how far I agree with someone before remembering to say anything positive about their view, which often makes people defensive. It's been a very long process for me to try and improve that.

I started by trying to make sure to add what I agreed with explicitly at the end, but it seems like people sometimes take that as patronizing, as if it were just an afterthought. Then I tried putting it at the front, but because it takes up so much less space than a nuanced discussion of why I disagree with the parts that I do, that people forget I even said something positive at all, and get defensive anyway. I'm STILL trying to learn how to properly incorporate this technique, but when I found out about "the compliment sandwich," where you both start AND end with the positive bits when you need to critique or disagree, I saw a much better response in most conversations.

These are the easiest (and best) cookies ever!

Preheat your oven to 350 ( do not put cookies in over before preheat is complete or you'll get some flat jacks)

Cover the batter balls completely and place them about 1 and 1/2 inches apart (give them room to breath)

Bake for 10 minutes. Do not wait for signs of being done, they will just burn on the bottom. Trust my ten minutes rule.

Let cool or eat warm with a glass of milk! You won't be able to stop at just 1!
